Reading · the episode that never ends

1.1 Discuss. How many episodes of a series have you watched in one evening? What made you stop — or what stopped you?

KEY WORDS

a cliffhanger an ending that leaves you unsure

to be hooked to be unable to stop

autoplay the next episode starts by itself

a habit something you do without deciding

The Episode That Never Ends

Nobody decides to watch five episodes. That is the first thing to understand about binge watching: the decision is not made once, at the start of the evening. It is made five times, and each time it is made a little more quickly than the last.

The mechanism is simple and it is not accidental. An episode ends on a cliffhanger; a counter appears in the corner of the screen; and unless something is done, the next episode is started for you. Ten seconds is not enough time to decide anything. It is, however, exactly enough time to fail to decide, and failing to decide is how most of us end up watching television until one in the morning.

This has been criticised, loudly, by doctors. The complaints are always the same three: viewers stop moving, viewers stop sleeping, and viewers report a strange flatness when a long series finally ends. In one American study, three-quarters of adults under thirty admitted that they had cancelled other plans in order to keep watching. The word admitted is doing some work there. Nobody says it proudly.

The defence is worth hearing, though, because it is not stupid. A good series is a long story, and nobody has ever been told that finishing a novel in one sitting is a health problem. The pleasure is the same pleasure. What has changed is not our behaviour but the delivery: the whole book is now handed to us at once, and a page turns itself every ten seconds.

So the sensible advice is not watch less. It is decide once. Set the number of episodes before you start. Turn autoplay off, so that the ten seconds becomes a real question instead of a countdown. Watch somewhere that is not your bedroom. And take a ten-minute break between episodes — not because ten minutes is restful, but because it is long enough for the cliffhanger to lose its grip.

Grammar · the passive

PRESENTATION

Form: be + past participle. The tense lives in be, not in the participle.

A Why we use it. Because we don't know who did it — My bike was stolen. Because it is obvious — He was arrested last night. Because it is not important — The series was filmed in Iceland.

B Because the topic is the object. Active: Doctors have criticised binge watching. Passive: Binge watching has been criticised by doctors. The passive lets you start the sentence with what you are talking about.

C by = who or what did it. The first episode was directed by Martin Scorsese.

D with = what was used. The whole episode was filmed with a smartphone camera.

No agent at all is the normal case. If by … adds nothing, leave it out: The results will be announced tomorrow — nobody needs by the committee.

Tense

Active

Passive

present simple

A computer creates the effects.

The effects are created by a computer.

present continuous

They are making more series.

More series are being made.

past simple

The channels controlled viewing.

Viewing was controlled by the channels.

past continuous

They were repairing my car.

My car was being repaired.

present perfect

Doctors have criticised it.

It has been criticised by doctors.

will

They will build a bridge.

A bridge will be built.

modal

You can reduce the effects.

The effects can be reduced.

ERROR WARNING

Four things go wrong, and they go wrong in this order of frequency:

1 Leaving out be, or getting the agreement wrong. All the children given a present. ✗ → All the children are given a present. ✓ · The letter were sent yesterday. ✗ → The letter was sent yesterday. ✓

2 A passive where the verb is not passive at all. The situation was changed last year. ✗ → The situation changed last year. ✓ · We have been thought it was a good idea. ✗ → We thought it was a good idea. ✓ Change and think are doing the action here; nothing is being done to them.

3 would instead of will. The results would announced tomorrow. ✗ → The results will be announced tomorrow. ✓

4 An active form where you need the future passive. It will send to you this afternoon. ✗ → It will be sent to you this afternoon. ✓

PRONUNCIATION — THE AUXILIARIES DISAPPEAR

In a passive sentence the meaning sits in the participle, so the auxiliaries are weak: has been criticised → /əzbɪn krɪtɪsaɪzd/ · are being made → /əbiːɪŋ meɪd/ · will be sent → /ləbi sent/.

This is why students hear criticised but not has been, and then write Binge watching criticised by doctors. The missing words were never loud enough to notice.

Vocabulary · -ed / -ing adjectives, and talking about what you watch

PRESENTATION

Two endings, two jobs. Get them the wrong way round and you say the opposite of what you mean.

-ing -ing describes the thing. I found the film boring. · That's a fascinating idea. · The trailer was disappointing.

-ed -ed describes how a person feels. I was so bored that I fell asleep. · I'm fascinated by it. · I was disappointed.

! So I am boring means you are dull company. I am bored means you have nothing to do. Both are correct English; only one of them is what your student meant.

The set: amusing / amused · boring / bored · depressing / depressed · disappointing / disappointed · fascinating / fascinated · interesting / interested · motivating / motivated

The thing (-ing)

The person (-ed)

The programme was disappointing.

I was disappointed by the programme.

It's a fascinating subject.

I'm fascinated by the subject.

The results were motivating.

I felt motivated to keep studying.

Winter can be depressing.

He gets depressed in winter.

PRONUNCIATION — THE -ED ENDING

Exactly the same three endings as a regular past simple verb:

/d/ after a voiced sound — amused · bored

/t/ after a voiceless sound — depressed

/ɪd/ after t or d — disappointed · interested · fascinated · motivated

The rule is mechanical: look at the sound before the -ed, not the spelling. Four of the seven adjectives in this set end in t, which is why so many of them take the extra syllable.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

The passive auxiliaries vanish. these people were asked which films → /wərɑːskt/ — two words, one syllable, no stress at all. Students hear asked and reconstruct an active sentence with the wrong subject.

And -ed adds a syllable you weren't expecting. fascinated is four syllables; bored is one. In a list — amused or fascinated or bored — the rhythm is uneven, and the short one is easy to lose.

RECOMMENDING AND RESPONDING

Giving a recommendation or an opinion: It's meant to be excellent. · It's supposed to be really good. · It was highly recommended by … · They've had great reviews. · Why don't we go and see …? · I think you'd love it.

Responding: That's a great idea! · I'm not a big fan of classical music. · I doubt he'd be interested. · It sounds really interesting, but …

The two to learn first are meant to be and supposed to be. Both mean people say it is — you are passing on somebody else's opinion, not giving your own. That is why the stress falls on meant and supposed.

PRONUNCIATION — SHOWING CONTRAST

When you correct somebody, the contrasting word takes extra stress. Everything else stays quiet.

— You like classical music, don't you? — No. Tom likes classical music. I like rock music. → the contrast is who.

— Does Tom like pop music? — No, Tom likes classical music. → the contrast is what.

Same words, different stress, different meaning. Say the second one with the stress on Tom and you have answered a question nobody asked.

You need these because you will be talking to two people at once — one on the phone, one in the room.

Hang on a moment / a minute / a second. · Wait a moment / a minute / a sec. · Just a moment. · Let me check (for you). One moment, please is the formal one — a receptionist says it, a friend does not.
